scenes.name: Soul sureño: Stax, Atlantic y FAME
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Stax era un negocio familiar en un viejo cine de Memphis, de dueños blancos (Jim Stewart y Estelle Axton) con una banda de estudio integrada (Steve Cropper, Isaac Hayes, Al Jackson, Duck Dunn, Booker T.) y solo artistas negros: ritmo pesado y vientos ásperos. Jerry Wexler llevó allí a Wilson Pickett, bailó el Jerk para enseñar el contratiempo de «In the Midnight Hour» y, cuando Stax lo vetó, lo llevó a los FAME de Rick Hall en Muscle Shoals, donde acababan de grabar «When a Man Loves a Woman» de Percy Sledge. Con una banda casi toda blanca (Spooner Oldham, Roger Hawkins) y pastillas, Pickett convirtió un estándar de cuatro años en la versión definitiva de «Land of 1000 Dances» (julio de 1966): gritos afinados, ritmo frenético, el «na, na-ne-na-na», un fragmento de un show que podría durar horas; parte de un continuo de la cultura negra entre el orgullo y la rabia. Otis Redding, heredero de Sam Cooke tras su asesinato, rompió con «I’ve Been Loving You Too Long» y Otis Blue fijó la palabra «soul», pero Stax no vendía como Motown hasta que Sam & Dave triunfaron con «Hold On! I’m Comin’». Los Beatles quisieron grabar en Stax en abril de 1966; su sonido está por todo Rubber Soul. La revista de Stax en Watts coincidió con los disturbios de agosto de 1965.

scenes.name: Stax
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: El imperio de Otis Redding, Booker T & the MGs, Johnnie Taylor, Rufus y Carla Thomas, los Staple Singers, Isaac Hayes y Albert King, capaz de rivalizar con Motown en ventas, con un sonido campestre y frito más pensado para el público negro. Frente al montaje mecánico de Motown, en Stax se grababa todo junto: «toca lo que sientas» (Otis Redding). «Tramp» de Otis y Carla, con el bajo más grave de la radio, es proto-funk puro; Johnnie Taylor llevó la sordidez sexual al soul («Who’s Making Love», «Disco Lady» con Bootsy al bajo); Rufus Thomas, payaso de «Do the Funky Chicken», hizo un poco más aceptable ser funky. Los MGs eran groove fluido más que bomba funk («Hip Hug-Her», «Melting Pot»), y los Bar-Kays originales («Soul Finger») habrían sido reyes de Memphis si no hubieran muerto con Otis en 1967.

podcast.title: "Last Night" Authorship Theory
podcast.body: Steve Cropper attributed the success of The Mar-Keys' instrumental "Last Night" to its danceability, specifically its suitability for the twist craze. "Steve Krupper always argued that it was because you could dance the twist to it, and so it wrote the twist craze"

podcast.title: Early Band Leadership
podcast.body: Steve Cropper led The Royal Spades, an all-white group passionate about R&B. He played guitar in the band, which later welcomed Charles Axton and evolved into The Mar-Keys. "The group was led by guitarist Steve Cropper"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 105: "Green Onions" by Booker T.and the MGs

podcast.title: Origins of "Green Onions"
podcast.body: Cropper remembered a distinct musical lick he and Booker T. Jones had heard on the radio, but couldn't identify the song. This lick became the foundation for "Green Onions," which they improvised into a 12-bar instrumental during an unplanned session. "Cropper remembered a little musical lick he'd heard on the radio one day when he'd been driving with Booker."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 105: "Green Onions" by Booker T.and the MGs

podcast.title: Producer Role Post-Moman
podcast.body: After Chips Moman's departure from Stax, Steve Cropper shared the production duties with Jim Stewart. Cropper had been diligently learning how to make records and was well-equipped to take on this responsibility. "Jim Stewart and Steve Cropper split the production duties that Momen had had between them."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 105: "Green Onions" by Booker T.and the MGs

podcast.title: Quitting The Mar-Keys Tour
podcast.body: Cropper left The Mar-Keys' tour to promote "Last Night" due to resentment over the other teenage band members' unruly behavior and a leadership conflict between himself and Charles Axton. He returned to Memphis to work in the record shop and play on Stax sessions. "Kropper soon got tired of the tour, quit the group, and came back to Memphis."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 105: "Green Onions" by Booker T.and the MGs

podcast.title: Reasons for Duck Dunn Replacing Louis Steinberg
podcast.body: Cropper stated that Louis Steinberg was replaced by Duck Dunn in Booker T and the M.G.'s because Dunn's "hard-eared style" better suited their music. He also mentioned that Dunn was his best friend and he wanted to play more with him, implicitly downplaying Steinberg's claim of racial motivation. "Krupper has always said, he was because Duck Dunn had a hard-eared style that fit their music better than Steinberg's Lucifer Hill, but also that Dunn had been his best friend for years and he wanted to play more with him."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 105: "Green Onions" by Booker T.and the MGs

podcast.title: Songwriting Credits
podcast.body: Steve Cropper co-wrote several influential soul classics, including "In the Midnight Hour," "Dock of the Bay," and "Knock on Wood," showcasing his significant talent as a songwriter for Stax. "even the man who co-wrote in the midnight hour, Doc of the Bay, and Knock on Ward, had his off days."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 105: "Green Onions" by Booker T.and the MGs

podcast.title: Studio and Record Shop Contributions
podcast.body: Cropper assisted in refurbishing the cinema into the Stax recording studio and worked in Estelle Axton's record shop, often helping behind the counter. This dual role made him readily available for studio sessions. "Cropper and Charles Axton helped with the refurbishing of the cinema into a recording studio."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 105: "Green Onions" by Booker T.and the MGs

podcast.title: Unsuccessful Country Production
podcast.body: Steve Cropper produced "The Three Dogwoods" by Nick Charles, a novelty country song told from the perspective of the tree used for Jesus's crucifixion. This record was a commercial failure, demonstrating that even prolific songwriters like Cropper had "off days." "That was Covid and by Cropper, which shows that even the man who co-wrote in the midnight hour, Doc of the Bay, and Knock on Ward, had his off days."
